tur18-0: Iliotibial Band Syndrome (Runner's Knee): Causes, Treatment and Exercises | İhsan Eren
tur18-1: Iliotibial band syndrome: what causes pain on the outside of the knee, risk factors, treatment, hip strengthening exercises and a safe return to running.
tur18-3: Pain that starts on the outside of the knee while running, often at the same point in the run and easing when you stop, is often caused by iliotibial band syndrome. It is the most common complaint on the outside of the knee in runners. This guide explains where the pain comes from, why it develops, how it is treated and how you can return to running safely.
tur18-5: Frequency of iliotibial band syndrome in runners (systematic review)
tur18-6: The most common knee pain in runners after pain at the front of the knee
tur18-7: Runners back to pain-free running after a 6-week hip strengthening programme (small, uncontrolled study)

tur18-9: Where does the pain come from?
tur18-10: The iliotibial band is a thick strip of connective tissue running from the outside of the hip to the outside of the knee. For many years the pain was thought to come from the band rubbing over a bony bump at the knee. Cadaver and MRI studies, however, showed that the band is firmly anchored to the thigh bone and does not really slide over the bone. The pain may instead come from compression of a layer of fat, rich in nerves and blood vessels, beneath the band when the knee is bent at about 30 degrees.
tur18-11: Sharp or aching pain on the outside of the knee; it sometimes spreads up or down.
tur18-12: The pain often starts at the same point in every run and eases when you stop.
tur18-13: Running downhill and running longer than usual make the pain worse.
tur18-14: If it gets worse, there can also be pain when walking or sitting with the knee bent.
tur18-16: It is an overuse injury, seen most often in runners and cyclists. Evidence on its causes is limited and conflicting, but these factors stand out:
tur18-17: Increasing load quickly: In a study following 874 novice runners, distance-related injuries, including this syndrome, were more common in those who increased their weekly distance by more than 30% over two weeks; the difference was at the borderline of statistical significance.
tur18-18: Hip and knee movements: In a review combining 13 studies, female runners who developed the syndrome had more inward movement of the hip, more inward rotation of the knee and more sideways lean of the trunk while running.
tur18-19: Weak hip muscles: Runners with the syndrome were shown to have weaker muscles that move the hip out to the side on the painful side; but it is not clear whether this is a cause or a result.
tur18-20: Others: Worn-out shoes, slippery or sloping ground and long downhill runs.
tur18-21: If the pain is mild, finish your run before the point where it starts; if it is severe, stop the activity causing it for a while and keep fit with a pain-free exercise.
tur18-22: You can apply ice wrapped in a cloth or a cold compress for 15–20 minutes every few hours. If you want to use a painkiller, ask your doctor or pharmacist.
tur18-23: The approach used most often in research, and with the most consistent results, is strengthening the muscles that move the hip out to the side. In a 2024 review of 13 studies, pain fell markedly over 2–8 weeks when strengthening was used on its own or together with manual therapy or shockwave therapy.
tur18-24: In recent-onset symptoms, a steroid injection may reduce pain in the first two weeks; its long-term effect is unknown.
tur18-25: Rarely; considered only for symptoms that persist despite months of appropriate treatment.
tur18-26: Studies on the treatment of this syndrome are small and generally of low quality. That is why most of the advice relies on load management and hip strengthening, where the evidence is strongest.
tur18-27: Six exercises for iliotibial band syndrome
tur18-28: These movements aim to strengthen the muscles that move the hip out to the side and your control of the pelvis and knee while running. The numbers of repetitions are general suggestions. The movements may feel like effort, but they should not increase the pain on the outside of your knee.
tur18-29: Lie on your pain-free side with your lower knee slightly bent. Keeping your top leg straight and slightly behind you, with your toes pointing forwards, slowly lift and lower it. You should feel a burn at the side of your hip.
tur18-31: Lie on your side with your elbow under your shoulder and your knees bent. Lift your hips off the floor to make a straight line from your head to your knees and hold. When it gets easier, straighten your knees and do it on your feet.
tur18-33: Lie on your back with your knees bent and feet on the floor. Squeeze your buttocks and lift your hips, hold briefly and lower slowly. When it gets easier, do it on one leg.
tur18-35: Stand on one foot. Keep your pelvis level and do not let your knee drop inwards. If needed, hold on lightly to a worktop; when it gets easier, close your eyes or try it on a soft surface.
tur18-36: Stand with your back against a wall and your feet hip-width apart. Bend and straighten your knees to a pain-free depth, with your knees tracking over your second toe. Make sure your knees do not drop inwards.
tur18-38: Once you can walk without pain, start by alternating short bouts of running with walking on flat ground. Stop before the point where the pain starts; leave downhill running until last.
tur18-39: Increase the running bouts a little each session; every other day
tur18-40: To interpret pain during exercise, see the exercise pain traffic light; for hip and knee control, see balance training.
tur18-41: Do I need to stop running completely?
tur18-42: Usually not, but you need to reduce the load. A UK health provider's information page suggests that if the pain is mild you finish your run before the point where it usually starts, and if it is severe you stop the activity causing it for a while. Meanwhile you can stay fit with swimming or other exercise that does not hurt.
tur18-43: Do stretching or foam rolling help?
tur18-44: They may feel relieving, but they do not lengthen the iliotibial band. A review of 13 studies found no evidence that stretching changes the band's length. The band is a thick strip of connective tissue firmly anchored to the thigh bone; the most evidence is for programmes based on strengthening the hip muscles.
tur18-46: It may give short-term relief. In a small study of 18 runners with recent-onset symptoms, a steroid injection into the area reduced pain while running in the first two weeks more than an injection of local anaesthetic alone. Its long-term effect is unknown, and an injection does not replace adjusting your load and a strengthening programme. Make this decision together with your doctor.
tur18-47: How long does it take to get better?
tur18-48: Most people can return to running within 6–8 weeks. At the end of a 6-week programme focused on strengthening the hip muscles, 22 of 24 runners were back to pain-free running and the problem had not returned 6 months later; however, this was a small study without a control group. If you have had the pain for a long time, recovery may take longer.
tur18-49: Do I need to change my shoes?
tur18-50: Worn-out shoes are listed among the risk factors. Your physiotherapist may look at how you run and suggest changes to your shoes or running technique. Evidence for changing running technique is so far limited to a few case reports.
tur18-51: Rarely. Surgery is considered only for symptoms that persist despite months of appropriate treatment. Studies on treating iliotibial band syndrome in runners are generally of low quality, so load management and exercise are tried first.

tur18-63: Exercise and breathing in long COVID: post-exertional symptom exacerbation, what to check before exercising, pacing, the research and six gentle movements at home.
tur18-64: Exercise and breathing in long COVID
tur18-65: For people who have fatigue, breathlessness and difficulty thinking for months after COVID-19, movement can be an important part of recovery; but at the wrong dose it can make symptoms flare. This guide explains what long COVID is, what to look out for before you start exercising, how to pace your energy and gentle movements you can do at home.
tur18-66: Estimated share of people infected with COVID-19 up to the end of 2021 who developed long COVID (about 145 million people)
tur18-67: Share of these people still with symptoms 12 months later
tur18-69: Extra gain on a walking test with 3 months of personalised resistance exercise, compared with usual care
tur18-70: People rating their health as “much better” 3 months after an 8-week online group programme, compared with the control group
tur18-72: According to the World Health Organization's definition, long COVID (post COVID-19 condition) consists of symptoms that usually appear 3 months after the start of the infection, last at least 2 months and cannot be explained by another illness. Symptoms may be new or may have continued since the illness; ups and downs and relapses are common. The UK guideline (NICE) calls symptoms lasting 4–12 weeks “ongoing symptomatic COVID-19” and those lasting more than 12 weeks “post-COVID-19 syndrome”.
tur18-73: The most common symptoms are fatigue, breathlessness and difficulty with attention and memory; these can markedly affect daily life.
tur18-75: The World Health Organization and World Physiotherapy recommend that the following are assessed before you start exercising:
tur18-76: Post-exertional symptom exacerbation: a marked worsening after physical, mental or social effort, often appearing 12 hours or more later.
tur18-77: Oxygen falling with effort: a drop of 3 points or more in oxygen saturation during or after mild effort should be investigated.
tur18-78: Heart problems: if you have chest pain, palpitations or unexplained breathlessness, your heart needs to be assessed first.
tur18-79: Dizziness on standing: if you have palpitations, dizziness or feel faint, you may need to start with exercises done lying down or sitting.
tur18-81: For people with post-exertional symptom exacerbation, the World Health Organization recommends education in energy conservation and pacing, rather than pushing exercise. For fatigue, it recommends a cautious return to exercise adjusted to symptoms, together with pacing.
tur18-83: When your symptoms start to rise, take a break from the activity; do not push through to the end.
tur18-85: Build regular rest breaks into your day; rest before you get tired, not only once you are tired.
tur18-87: Spread heavy tasks across the day and the week, and do not overdo it on good days either. Use a diary to track which activities increase your symptoms the next day.
tur18-88: World Physiotherapy recommends that graded exercise programmes, which increase time or load at set intervals regardless of symptoms, are not used in long COVID, and that activity is adjusted each day according to symptoms.
tur18-89: In a randomised trial in Scotland with 233 people whose symptoms had lasted at least 4 weeks, personalised resistance exercises done at home every day for 3 months (lying down for those confined to bed, otherwise sitting or standing; arm exercises first, leg exercises from the third week) increased the distance on a walking test by an average of 36.5 metres compared with usual care. Grip strength, quality of life, and anxiety and depression symptoms also improved; fatigue and breathlessness measures did not differ.
tur18-90: In the REGAIN study of 585 people who had been in hospital with COVID-19 and had had problems for more than 3 months, an 8-week online, supervised group exercise and psychological support programme improved quality of life over a year; at 3 months 17% rated their health as “much better”, compared with 8%, and there was no sign that the programme caused harm. How far these results apply to people who were not in hospital and who have marked post-exertional flares is not known.
tur18-91: Six gentle movements for long COVID
tur18-92: The first three movements help manage breathlessness; the last three help you slowly regain strength and stamina. Do the last three only if you do not have post-exertional symptom exacerbation or your healthcare team has agreed. Adjust the dose to your symptoms each day: if your symptoms rise the next day, do less next time.
tur18-93: Sit comfortably, relax your shoulders and put one hand on your belly. Breathe in slowly through your nose and feel your belly rise, then breathe out slowly through your mouth. Do not force your breath.
tur18-94: A few minutes, several times a day
tur18-95: Breathe in through your nose, then purse your lips as if to whistle and breathe out slowly, taking about twice as long as you did to breathe in. You can use it when breathless or climbing stairs.
tur18-97: When you are short of breath, sit and lean forward, resting your elbows on your knees or a table. Relax your shoulders and breathe slowly in and out; carry on once your breathing settles.
tur18-99: Stand up from a sturdy chair and sit down with control. Do this only if you do not get a marked worsening after exercise; adjust the number to that day's energy.
tur18-100: Few enough that you do not feel worse the next day; for example, start with 5 repetitions
tur18-101: Place your hands on a wall at chest height, bend your elbows to bring your chest towards the wall and push back. You can also start with arm exercises sitting or lying down.
tur18-102: According to your symptoms; start with a few repetitions
tur18-103: Take short walks around the house or nearby. If your symptoms do not get worse the next day, increase the time very slightly; on bad days, do less.
tur18-104: Short bouts adjusted to your symptoms
tur18-105: To relax, see the physiological sigh; to track your symptoms, see the pain diary.
tur18-107: In some people, yes. In some people with long COVID, symptoms worsen markedly after physical, mental or social effort, often 12 hours or more later; this is called post-exertional symptom exacerbation. World Physiotherapy recommends asking about it before recommending exercise. If you have it, pacing your energy should come before pushing exercise.
tur18-109: It means planning your activities to stay within a limit that does not trigger your symptoms. It is not avoiding activity; it is making progress without overdoing it on good days, with rest breaks built into the day. When your symptoms start to rise, stop, rest and rearrange your plan. A diary or an app can help you recognise your limit.
tur18-111: It is not recommended for people with post-exertional symptom exacerbation. World Physiotherapy recommends that programmes increasing time or load at set intervals regardless of symptoms are not used in long COVID, and that activity continuously adjusted to symptoms is preferred.
tur18-112: What should be checked before starting exercise?
tur18-113: The World Health Organization strongly recommends that oxygen falling with effort and heart problems are investigated and treated before an exercise programme is started. Dizziness, palpitations or feeling faint on standing should also be assessed; in that case you may need to start with exercises done lying down or sitting.
tur18-114: Has exercise been shown to help?
tur18-115: In some groups, yes. In a study of 233 people in Scotland, personalised resistance exercises done every day for 3 months increased walking distance by an average of 36.5 metres compared with usual care and improved grip strength, quality of life, and anxiety and depression symptoms; however, fatigue measures did not differ. In another study of 585 people who had been in hospital with COVID, 8 weeks of online group exercise and psychological support improved quality of life over a year.
tur18-116: It varies a great deal from person to person. According to estimates reported by the World Health Organization, about 3.7% of those infected up to the end of 2021 developed long COVID, and 15% of them still had symptoms 12 months later. Most people improve over time; ups and downs in symptoms are common.

tur18-129: Preventing Muscle Loss on Weight-Loss Medication (GLP-1): Exercise and Protein | İhsan Eren
tur18-130: Limiting muscle loss while taking weight-loss medicines such as semaglutide and tirzepatide: the research, guidelines, strength exercise, protein and six exercises at home.
tur18-131: Protect your muscles while taking weight-loss medication
tur18-132: GLP-1 medicines such as semaglutide and tirzepatide produce substantial weight loss in the treatment of obesity. But with rapid weight loss, muscle can be lost along with fat, which can affect strength and mobility. This guide explains why strength exercise, enough protein and regular activity matter for protecting your muscles while taking these medicines, and six exercises you can do at home.
tur18-134: People living with obesity worldwide (World Health Organization)
tur18-135: Average fall in fat mass and in lean tissue mass in the semaglutide trial
tur18-136: Estimated share of weight lost with these medicines that comes from lean tissue
tur18-137: Share of lost weight regained in the year after stopping the medicine (semaglutide trial)
tur18-138: Why is muscle lost during weight loss?
tur18-139: When the body takes in less energy, it uses lean tissue, including muscle, as well as fat. In the 140 people whose body composition was measured in the large semaglutide trial, fat mass fell by 19.3% and lean tissue mass by 9.7% in those taking the medicine. Because more fat was lost, the proportion of lean tissue in the body rose; in other words, body composition improved overall.
tur18-140: Even so, part of the lean tissue lost is muscle. Muscle matters for strength, balance, blood sugar use and independence in later life. That is why protecting muscle matters even more in older age, in people whose muscle mass is already low and in those who are inactive.
tur18-142: World Health Organization (2025): states that GLP-1 medicines may be used for the long-term treatment of obesity in adults, and that intensive behavioural support such as healthy eating and physical activity programmes may be offered alongside them. It stresses that the medicine alone is not enough and that long-term data are limited.
tur18-143: US nutrition and obesity societies (2025): recommend strength exercise and enough protein to limit muscle and bone loss during weight loss; monitoring for deficiencies of iron, B vitamins, calcium and vitamin D; and managing gastrointestinal side effects.
tur18-144: General recommendation: The World Health Organization recommends 150–300 minutes of moderate aerobic activity a week for adults, plus strength exercise for the major muscle groups on at least 2 days a week.
tur18-146: In Denmark, 195 people who had lost an average of 13.1 kg on a low-calorie diet were assigned for a year to exercise, liraglutide, both, or placebo. Compared with placebo, the exercise group weighed 4.1 kg less, the liraglutide group 6.8 kg less and those doing both 9.5 kg less. Body fat percentage fell most, by 3.9 points, in those doing both; the only group that preserved lean tissue was the exercise group.
tur18-147: In a 6-month study of 160 frail adults over 65 with obesity, those who combined weight loss with both aerobic and strength exercise improved their physical function the most.
tur18-148: No completed study has yet tested how well strength exercise protects muscle while taking semaglutide or tirzepatide; a randomised trial of 232 people is under way. That trial aims for strength exercise at home 3 days a week and 1.6 grams of protein per kilogram of body weight a day.
tur18-150: Do exercises that work the major muscle groups on at least 2–3 days a week. Do each set until the last few repetitions feel hard; increase the resistance as it gets easier.
tur18-151: When your appetite is low, eat protein-rich foods first; add a protein source to every meal.
tur18-152: Keep active every day with at least 150 minutes a week of brisk walking or a similar activity.
tur18-154: Tell your team if you have nausea, constipation or diarrhoea; eating small amounts often can help.
tur18-156: Track your strength as well as your weight; for example, repeat the 30-second chair test every few weeks.
tur18-157: Six exercises to protect your muscles
tur18-158: The first five movements are strength exercises for the leg, hip, chest, back and calf muscles; the sixth supports daily activity. The numbers of repetitions are general suggestions; if you are just starting or have a health condition, plan your programme with your doctor or physiotherapist.
tur18-159: Sit at the front of a sturdy chair. Without using your hands, stand up as you breathe out and sit down slowly. When it gets easier, hold a weight such as a water bottle or use a lower chair.

tur18-164: Walk at a pace where you can talk but are slightly out of breath. It is an easy way to stay active on days when you are not doing strength exercises.
tur18-165: At least 150 minutes a week; spread across the days
tur18-166: For a weekly strength programme, see the home strength circuit; for more on muscle loss, see the sarcopenia guide.
tur18-167: How much muscle will I lose on weight-loss medication?
tur18-168: It varies from person to person. In the body composition measurements of the large semaglutide trial, fat mass fell by 19.3% and lean (including muscle) tissue mass by 9.7%. Because more fat was lost, the proportion of lean tissue in the body actually rose. Researchers estimate that about 15–50% of the weight lost with these medicines comes from lean tissue.
tur18-170: Some loss of lean tissue is expected when losing weight. But strength and mobility matter, especially in older age and in people whose muscle mass is already low. In a study of 160 older adults with obesity, those who combined weight loss with aerobic and strength exercise improved their physical function the most.
tur18-171: How much protein should I eat?
tur18-172: US nutrition and obesity societies recommend getting enough protein alongside strength exercise to limit muscle loss. When your appetite is low, adding a protein source (eggs, yoghurt, cheese, pulses, meat, chicken or fish) to every meal helps. An ongoing study is aiming for 1.6 grams of protein per kilogram of body weight a day. If you have kidney disease, decide on your protein intake with your doctor.
tur18-173: Does exercise boost the effect of the medicine?
tur18-174: One study supports this. When 195 people who had lost an average of 13 kg on a low-calorie diet were followed for a year, those who kept the weight off best were those combining liraglutide with exercise: they weighed 9.5 kg less than with placebo, and their body fat percentage fell the most. The only group that preserved lean tissue was the exercise group.
tur18-175: What happens when I stop the medicine?
tur18-176: Some of the weight may come back. In a study following 327 people who stopped semaglutide after 68 weeks, about two thirds of the weight lost was regained within a year, and the improvements in cardiovascular health largely went back to where they started. That is why it matters to build strength exercise and eating habits while you are taking the medicine.
tur18-177: Has the benefit of strength exercise with these medicines been proven?
tur18-178: Not fully yet. According to the authors of a study protocol published in 2026, no completed study has tested the effect of strength exercise while taking semaglutide or tirzepatide; a study of 232 people is under way to answer this. Even so, it is well established that strength exercise protects muscle during diet-induced weight loss, and guidelines recommend strength exercise alongside these medicines.

In a meta-analysis combining 4 trials in amateur and sub-elite footballers, this warm-up programme reduced injuries by 39%, knee injuries by 48% and hamstring injuries by 60%. In a study of 1,892 female footballers aged 13–17 in Norway, severe injuries fell by 45%.
tur18-277: The programme recommends doing it at the start of every training session and at least twice a week. Only 13% of the teams in the meta-analysis reached this frequency; in real life, the hardest part is doing it regularly. Before matches, only the running parts (parts 1 and 3) are done.
tur18-278: I don't play football. Is it suitable for me?
tur18-279: The programme was developed for football and most of the evidence comes from football. But its structure, with running, changing direction, jumping and landing and a hamstring exercise, is also used in sports with similar movements such as basketball, volleyball and handball. A physiotherapist can help you adapt the programme to your sport.
tur18-280: The Nordic hamstring is very hard. What should I do?
tur18-281: At first, do only a few repetitions and lean forwards only as far as you can control. In a meta-analysis of 15 studies and 8,459 athletes, programmes including this exercise roughly halved hamstring injuries. Delayed muscle soreness at the back of the thigh is common in the first weeks; increase the repetitions slowly.
tur18-282: When should I move up a level?
tur18-283: When you can do a movement for the stated time and repetitions without difficulty and with good technique. The programme manual says teams can usually progress together after 3–4 weeks. This page times the basic level; for the advanced levels, work with your coach or physiotherapist.

tur18-293: Daily step count is one of the easiest health measures to track. According to large studies, every extra step counts even for people who move very little, and most of the benefit starts well before 10,000 steps. This page suggests a realistic weekly target based on last week's average, maps out a plan to bring you closer to the thresholds seen in research and records your weekly averages.

tur18-323: In a 2025 review of 57 studies, people taking 7,000 steps a day had a 47% lower risk of death, a 47% lower risk of death from cardiovascular disease, a 38% lower risk of dementia, 22% fewer depressive symptoms and 28% fewer falls than those taking 2,000 steps. For death, cardiovascular disease, dementia and falls, most of the benefit appeared at around 5,000–7,000 steps.
tur18-324: These are observational studies: people who walk a lot may be healthier in other ways too. Even so, the results from different countries are consistent and show that even small increases matter.

More steps may bring extra benefit for some conditions, but 7,000 steps is a realistic and effective target for most people.
tur18-333: I'm older. Is my target different?
tur18-334: In an analysis combining 15 studies, the fall in risk of death levelled off at about 6,000–8,000 steps a day in people aged 60 and over, and at 8,000–10,000 steps in those under 60. This page shows your target according to these ranges for your age.
tur18-335: How much should I increase each day?
tur18-336: Small increases matter too. In a meta-analysis of about 227,000 people, every extra 1,000 steps was linked to about a 15% lower risk of death. This page suggests adding 1,000 steps to your daily average each week; this is a general suggestion, so if you have joint pain or a health condition, increase more slowly.
tur18-337: How do I measure my steps?
tur18-338: Your phone's health app or a step counter is enough. Take the daily average for the last 7 days; look at the weekly average rather than a single day. Times when you are not carrying your phone are not counted, so your real step count may be a little higher.
tur18-339: Does the pace of steps matter?
tur18-340: Total step count is the most consistent measure. In the 15-study analysis, the step rate in the fastest 30–60 minutes of the day was also linked to lower mortality, but time spent walking above a set pace was not significant on its own. Making some of your walks brisk still improves your fitness.

tur18-350: Exercise and intensive blood pressure and cholesterol treatment did not improve thinking skills over two years
tur18-351: 5 more minutes of movement a day: the big effect of small changes
tur18-352: In October 2026 the American Academy of Pain Medicine (AAPM) published a new clinical guideline for low back pain lasting less than 6 weeks and not caused by an injury. The guideline is based on a systematic review of 105 studies published in Pain Medicine. In people without signs of a serious condition, early imaging (X-ray, MRI) did not improve pain or function; the guideline makes a strong recommendation against routine imaging for them. Patient education, staying active with lighter activities and self-care are recommended first; if they can be used safely, short-term non-prescription painkillers (NSAIDs) and heat are also options. Opioids should not be used routinely as first treatment: they did not reduce pain more than placebo but caused more side effects. Paracetamol was no different from placebo. If the pain does not ease within 1–2 weeks or gets worse, at least one additional treatment, such as muscle relaxants, physical therapy or acupuncture, can be offered.
tur18-353: In the review, the benefit of early referral to physical therapy, manipulation and mobilisation, muscle relaxants and NSAIDs was rated with moderate confidence; but the benefits were generally small and appeared in the first few weeks. Psychosocial factors best predicted whether the pain would persist. In more than 85% of recent-onset low back pain there is no specific disease or spinal problem, and most people improve within days or weeks. The project that produced the guideline was funded by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA).
tur18-354: Sources: American Academy of Pain Medicine, 5 October 2026 · Pain Medicine, 2026 (systematic review) · Managed Healthcare Executive, 8 October 2026 · Medical Society of the State of New York, 9 October 2026
tur18-355: The rrAD study, run at four centres in the US and published in JAMA Neurology on 23 March 2026, included 513 people aged 60–85 without dementia but with high blood pressure, a family history of dementia or memory complaints they had noticed themselves. Participants were divided into four groups: about 160 minutes a week of moderate-to-vigorous aerobic exercise, intensive drug treatment aiming to bring systolic pressure below 130 and lower LDL cholesterol, both, or usual care. After two years, a composite score of thinking and memory tests rose slightly in all groups, but there was no significant difference between them. The drug treatment markedly lowered blood pressure and LDL cholesterol.
tur18-356: In the researchers' words, “we improved the body, but not the brain”. Two years may be too short to see an effect on preventing cognitive decline; participants were cognitively healthy at the start, and because scores rose in all groups it was harder to see a difference. The result does not mean that exercise and blood pressure control are worthless: both matter for cardiovascular health. The researchers stress that longer approaches targeting several risk factors together are needed to prevent dementia.
tur18-357: Sources: JAMA Neurology, March 2026 · Pennington Biomedical Research Center, 23 March 2026 · EMJ
tur18-359: An analysis published in The Lancet on 14 January 2026, combining cohorts of more than 135,000 adults from Norway, Sweden, the US and the UK whose activity was measured with devices, used an average of 8 years of follow-up data to estimate how many deaths small behaviour changes could prevent. If everyone except the most active 20% did 5 more minutes of moderate activity a day (such as brisk walking), about 10% of deaths could be prevented; with 10 extra minutes a day this rose to 15%. In the least active 20%, a 5-minute increase could prevent about 6% of deaths. Sitting 30 minutes less a day could prevent about 7% of deaths (3% in those who sit the most).
tur18-360: These are model estimates based on observational data; they do not prove that activity directly lowers the risk of death. Activity was measured only once at the start, unmeasured factors such as mobility limitations may have affected the results, and the data come only from high-income countries. Experts stress that the results should be read as a possible effect at population level, not as a personal exercise prescription. Still, the message is clear: you don't need to run marathons; even a few more minutes of brisk walking each day can make a difference.
tur18-361: Sources: The Lancet, 14 January 2026 · EurekAlert! (The Lancet), 13 January 2026 · Karolinska Institutet, 14 January 2026 · Science Media Centre Spain, expert reactions
